1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status current with `--status` and its strategy prose current with
60	  `--summary` / `--summary-file` (there is no `--strategy` flag). It doubles as
61	  the **project board**:
62	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
63	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
64	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
65	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
66	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
67	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
68	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
69	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
70	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
71	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
72	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
73	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
74	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
75	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
76	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
77	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
78	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
79	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
80	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
81	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
82	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
83	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
84	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
85	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
86	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
87	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
88	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
89	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
90	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
91	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
92	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
93	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
94	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
95	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
96	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
97	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
98	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
99	
100	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
101	
102	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
103	
104	| Variable | Meaning |
105	|---|---|
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
112	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
113	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
114	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
115	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
116	
117	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
118	
119	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
120	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
121	
122	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
123	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
124	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
125	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
126	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
127	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
128	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
129	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
130	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
131	
132	## One-shot discipline (important)
133	
134	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
135	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
136	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
137	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
138	
139	## Pick the highest-value work
140	
141	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
142	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
143	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
144	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
145	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
146	
147	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
148	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
149	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
150	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
151	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
152	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
153	(it returns to the queue).
154	
155	## Fresh-context checkpoints
156	
157	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
158	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
159	checkpoints:
160	
161	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
162	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
163	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
164	  clean/build result.
165	
166	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
167	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
168	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
169	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
170	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
171	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
172	terminal `done` claim.
173	
174	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
175	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
176	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
177	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
178	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
179	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
180	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
181	
182	## Warnings are work
183	
184	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
185	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
186	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
187	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
188	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
189	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
190	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
191	why.
192	
193	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
194	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
195	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
196	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
197	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
198	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
199	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
200	
201	## Do the work (Lean)
202	
203	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
204	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
205	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
206	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
207	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
208	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
209	configured final build covers the same files.
210	
211	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
212	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
213	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
214	mathlib — query it:
215	
216	| You want | Use | Not |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
219	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
220	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
221	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
222	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
223	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
224	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
225	
226	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
227	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
228	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
229	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
230	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
231	back to grep.
232	
233	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
234	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
235	
236	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
237	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
238	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
239	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
240	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
241	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
242	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
243	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
244	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
245	
246	## Read the other projects
247	
248	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
249	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
250	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
251	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
252	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
253	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
254	
255	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
256	
257	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
258	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
259	needs no permission.
260	
261	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
262	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
263	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
264	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
265	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
266	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
267	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
268	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
269	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
270	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
271	
272	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
273	
274	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
275	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
276	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
277	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
278	
279	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
280	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
281	
282	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status (`--status`) and strategy prose
283	  (`--summary`), not a re-narration of the diff.
284	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
285	  as **memory**.
286	
287	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
288	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
289	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
290	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
291	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
292	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
293	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
294	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
295	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
296	
297	## Resuming after an interruption
298	
299	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
300	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
301	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
302	
303	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
304	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
305	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
306	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
307	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
308	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
309	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
310	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
311	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
312	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
313	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
314	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
315	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
316	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
317	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
318	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
319	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
320	
321	## Final report (your last message)
322	
323	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
324	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
325	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
326	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
327	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
328	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
329	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
330	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
331	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
332	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
333	not by itself a reason to stop.
334	
335	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
336	
337	There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
338	and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
339	workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the

2	name: horizon-start
3	description: Work out which situation you were launched into — first round of a fresh run, a hand-off from the horizon session that just finished, a resume after a crash or pause, or a session outside any run — and pull exactly the context that situation calls for. Load at the START of a session, before picking up the task.
4	---
5	
6	Your prompt carries the task and nothing else: no history, no word about who ran
7	before you or how they ended. That is deliberate — state is pulled, not pushed
8	(the `horizon` skill's stance). But it means a session that starts working
9	immediately is guessing. Usually somebody *was* here before you, often minutes
10	ago, and their report was written for you.
11	
12	This skill is the first pass: four cheap reads, a guess at the situation, then
13	the context that situation actually calls for. Budget a couple of minutes, not a
14	tenth of the session.
15	
16	## The four signals
17	
18	```bash
19	ls "$ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR/.."     # sibling sessions in THIS run
20	"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json             # `paused` (why the last run stopped) + `recent_failure_reasons`
21	"$HORIZON_BIN" ps                       # is another run live on this workspace RIGHT NOW?
22	"$HORIZON_GIT" log --oneline -15        # what actually landed recently
23	```
24	
25	The sibling listing is the one that decides most of it. A run's sessions look
26	like:
27	
28	```
29	0001-system            ← orchestrator bookkeeping (commits, integration), not an agent
30	0002-horizon-PET.5     ← a horizon session; meta.json + transcript.jsonl + usage.json
31	0003-system
32	0004-horizon-PET.5     ← ...you, probably
33	```
34	
35	For any earlier `*-horizon-*` sibling, two files answer everything:
36	
37	- **`report.md` present** → that session finished on its own terms and wrote you
38	  a hand-off. **`report.md` absent** → it was killed mid-flight. This is the
39	  single most informative bit on disk.
40	- **`meta.json`** → `round`, `task_id`, `status`, `started_at`, `ended_at`,
41	  `model`. `ended_at` against the current time tells you whether "recent" means
42	  four minutes ago or last week.
43	
44	## Which situation am I in?
45	
46	Work down the list; the first match is your best guess.
47	
48	**An earlier horizon sibling has no `report.md`** → *resume after a crash or
49	kill.* Its work is half-done and possibly half-committed. Read its commits in
50	the ledger first (they are the part that survived), then the tail of its
51	transcript to see what it was in the middle of — `usage --json` `paused` gives
52	the reason it died (usage limit, budget, auth), and `recent_failure_reasons`
53	shows rate-limit pressure that may still be there. Trust the ledger over the
54	transcript: anything it did not commit is gone, no matter what it said it was
55	doing. If the dead session shares your `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK`, you are continuing
56	its exact work — pick up its front rather than opening a new one.
57	
58	**An earlier horizon sibling has a `report.md`** → *hand-off from the session
59	that just finished.* The common case. Read that report first — its `## Next` and
60	`## Why I stopped` were written for exactly this moment — then its commits, then
61	any inbox items addressed to horizon since its `ended_at`. Do not re-derive what
62	it already established; do not redo a piece it says is done without checking the
63	ledger.
64	
65	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is `0` and no horizon sibling exists** → *first agent
66	of the run.* Nobody handed you anything **in this run** — but the workspace is
67	almost never greenfield. Earlier runs live under `.archon-horizon/runs/`; the
68	roadmap, the inbox and the ledger carry their conclusions. Skim the roadmap and
69	recent ledger history before deciding a strategy that a previous run already
70	tried and rejected.
71	
72	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` is unset** → *not launched by the orchestrator* (an
73	interactive or hand-driven session). No run context exists to reconstruct;
74	orient from workspace state — roadmap, inbox, ledger — and say where things
75	stand before proposing work.
76	
77	One caveat about round numbers. `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is 0-based and reliable
78	for "am I first" — but a resumed run can re-run a round whose session died, so a
79	`0` with a dead sibling present means *resume*, not *fresh*. The dead-sibling
80	check settles it either way. (`ROUND + 1 == ROUNDS` is a sound last-round test,
81	resumed runs included — `ROUNDS` bounds the rounds *this* invocation drives, not
82	the run's original plan.)
83	
84	## Then, before you start
85	
86	- **`horizon ps` said another run is live?** You share one ledger branch with it.
87	  Commit in small coherent pieces and expect to see its commits interleaved.
88	- **Timestamps are context.** A predecessor that ended 90 seconds ago probably
89	  left a warm build; one that ended last week may have left a workspace that no
90	  longer compiles. Check rather than assume.
91	- **The inbox is the cross-session thread** — read what past sessions left for
92	  horizon, and the task's own comments if you share their `task_id`
93	  (`"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`). Skill:
94	  `horizon-inbox`.
95	
96	Then stop orienting and start working. The point of this pass is to begin from a
97	smarter place than round zero — not to reconstruct everything that ever happened
98	here.

38	later in `PARENT=$(… rev-parse HEAD)`. If another lane's CAS lands **between those two reads**,
39	your tree is built from the *old* snapshot while your parent is the *new* commit — and
40	`update-ref` **succeeds**, because it only checks that the ref has not moved since `rev-parse`.

93	2. **Before finishing, check and repair.** `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. status --porcelain | grep '^D'`
94	   must be empty. If it is not, repair with the **narrowest** form that covers your paths:
95	   `git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. reset -q -- <your project dir>/`. Prefer this to a whole-index
96	   `read-tree HEAD` when another run is live — a full reset can discard the other run's staging.

98	   that is only safe once you have confirmed the on-disk file is the one you want
99	   (`diff <(git --git-dir=$GD cat-file -p HEAD:<path>) <path>`).
100	
101	Expect to repeat step 2 more than once in a long session: every CAS commit by any lane re-stales
102	the index, so a repair done early does not stay done.

104	## 2. The lake mutex is a mkdir DIRECTORY lock — never flock a file there
105	
106	`/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock` is acquired by `mkdir` (atomic; a crash leaves a
107	directory that the next holder's timeout logic can reap). It is NOT a flock file: a lane
108	that runs `flock /tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock …` creates a plain FILE at the
109	path, and every mkdir-acquire loop then spins forever (this deadlocked all lanes
110	15:18–19:10 on 2026-07-16 until a human deleted it). Acquire pattern:
111	
112	```bash
113	LOCK=/tmp/claude-1001/ajcr-locks/lake.lock
114	while ! mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
115	  # (a) plain FILE at the path = a flock protocol-violation; reap immediately.
116	  if [ -f "$LOCK" ]; then echo "STALE: plain file at $LOCK (flock violation) — removing" >&2; rm -f "$LOCK"; continue; fi
117	  # (b) orphaned DIRECTORY from a crashed build (rmdir never ran). Reap on proof of death:
118	  if [ -d "$LOCK" ]; then
119	    holder=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)
120	    if [ -n "$holder" ] && ! kill -0 "$holder" 2>/dev/null; then
121	      echo "STALE: holder pid $holder dead — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
122	    fi
123	    # No pidfile (old-cohort holder): reap only if NO live lake build AND the dir is >15 min old.
124	    if [ -z "$holder" ] && ! pgrep -f 'lake build AlgebraicJacobian' >/dev/null 2>&1 \
125	       && [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null || date +%s) )) -gt 900 ]; then
126	      echo "STALE: no live build, lock >15min old — reaping" >&2; rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
127	    fi
128	  fi
129	  sleep 10
130	done
131	echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null      # record holder so a later reaper can prove liveness via kill -0
132	# … lake build … ; rm -rf "$LOCK"      # release (rm -rf, not rmdir — the pidfile makes the dir non-empty)
133	```

135	### 2a. THE RELEASE IS AS DANGEROUS AS THE REAP — check the pidfile before `rm -rf` (2026-07-28, run 0072)

137	The acquire loop above is careful; the release (`rm -rf "$LOCK"`) is not, and that asymmetry
138	caused a real incident. **A lane removed the lock directory while its pidfile named a LIVE pid
139	belonging to another lane's build**, having printed `ALIVE` for that pid one line earlier.
140	
141	The mechanism is worth stating because nothing in the recipe warns about it. The offending lane
142	had legitimately acquired the lock, and then **its own shell was killed by a harness timeout
143	while it held it**. On the next turn it reasoned "the lock is mine and my holder is dead, so
144	release it" — but in the interval a *different* lane had acquired the lock, so the pid in the
145	file had never been its own. The lane was running the release branch on a belief about history
146	rather than on a reading of the file.

149	> `[ "$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null)" = "$$" ] && rm -rf "$LOCK"`
150	> If it names anything else, the lock is not yours to release: say so and leave it alone.

154	* **"It was mine a minute ago" is not evidence**, especially when a harness can kill the shell
155	  between acquire and release. Every turn boundary is a window for another lane to take the lock.

158	  and hides the incident. Report it on the thread and let the owner re-take it.
159	
160	For long builds, prefer a form that cannot outlive its own hold: run the build detached with a
161	release trailing it in the *same* script, so the release is not a separate turn.

175	build temp dirs, and if Bash starts failing with quota errors, stop and report rather than

179	
180	`AlgebraicJacobian.lean` is edited by every lane. Committing the WHOLE file via any recipe

188	root file that references uncommitted files without naming that in the message.

191

193	2026-07-28: the diff printed a `-import`/`+import` pair from a sibling lane's *uncommitted*
194	worktree edit, the committing lane read it as background noise, and the commit published the
195	sibling's replacement — dropping `Picard/DivRepAffPullIndep.lean` from the import closure.
196	The file stayed in HEAD and still compiled, but was reachable from nothing: **un-rooted**,
197	i.e. I-0153 again, from a lane that had run the I-0153 check.

201	> **A `-import` line in that diff is never yours.** The only clean result is `+import <your
202	> file>` and nothing else. Any minus line means you are about to delete another lane's root
203	> entry — stop and explain it before committing. An unexplained `+import` you did not write
204	> is the same signal: a sibling's uncommitted edit is in your worktree copy, and a minus line
205	> usually accompanies it.

207	This is strictly stronger than "commit only your own lines", because you can intend that and
208	still sweep — staging the whole file is what publishes their edit, and the diff is your only
209	warning.

211	**Repair additively, never by reverting.** Restore the dropped import while **keeping** the
212	other lane's new one, then verify with a full root build (the 2026-07-28 repair: 9139 jobs,
213	exit 0, with the un-rooted file rebuilt). Reverting to your own earlier root blob discards
214	their work and turns one incident into two.

217	
218	No cross-workspace use (an OpenGA-Horizon agent squatted it ~25 min for its own

236	
237	§2's acquire recipe writes `$$` into `$LOCK/pid` so a later lane can prove death via

242	
243	Two consequences for a blocked lane, both applied in that incident:

245	* **Do not reap a directory whose holder you cannot prove dead**, even when you suspect a

247	* **Fall back to the narrowest check instead of blocking.** `lake env lean <file>` on the

249	  kernel check for that file. Record in the report that the mutex was unavailable and which
250	  check you substituted.

11	/-!
12	# The `Bool`-indexed family and selector of an affine two-chart cover (W5-T4, item (3a))
13	
14	Everything in `Tangent/TwoChartCechPic.lean` and its successors is stated for a family
15	`V : Bool → X.Opens` together with a selector `sel : X → Bool` satisfying `x ∈ V (sel x)`, and the
16	quotient-level results additionally need `Function.Surjective sel`. The Wave-5 consumer, by
17	contrast, holds a `Scheme.AffineTwoCover` (two named affine opens with affine overlap), which is
18	what `Cohomology/RelativeTwoCover.lean`'s `relCover` produces. This file is the bridge.
19	
20	## The finding: `hsel` is a real side condition, and it is exactly non-triviality
21	
22	`informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` §6.20(3a) flagged that selector surjectivity "is a real side
23	condition, not bookkeeping". Measured here, it is sharper than that: for the canonical selector
24	`sel x = if x ∈ V₀ then false else true`,
25	
26	```
27	Function.Surjective sel  ↔  V₀ ≠ ⊥ ∧ V₀ ≠ ⊤
28	```
29	
30	(`Scheme.AffineTwoCover.surjective_selector_iff`). Both directions are *genuine* content rather than
31	an artefact of this particular selector:
32	
33	* `V₀ = ⊥` makes `sel` constantly `true` — and then the "two-chart" cover is the one-chart cover
34	  `V₁ = ⊤`, whose Čech `Ȟ¹` is trivial for a different reason;
35	* `V₀ = ⊤` makes `sel` constantly `false`, i.e. `X` is covered by one *affine* chart, so `X` is
36	  affine.
37	
38	So a two-chart argument that needs `hsel` is asking for the cover to be **honestly two-chart**, and
39	that is the right hypothesis to carry rather than to hide. For the Wave-5 curve both conditions hold
40	— a curve is non-empty, and a proper positive-dimensional scheme over a field is not affine — but
41	neither is free, and neither is proved here: they are supplied by the consumer as
42	`h0 : V₀ ≠ ⊥` and `h1 : V₀ ≠ ⊤`.
43	
44	## Implementation notes
45	
46	The selector is defined by `Classical.dec`-backed `if x ∈ V₀`, so `hmem` is a two-case `split_ifs`
47	using `sup_eq_top` for the `x ∉ V₀` branch: a point of `⊤ = V₀ ⊔ V₁` outside `V₀` lies in `V₁`
48	(`TopologicalSpace.Opens.mem_sup`).
49	
50	The family is `boolFamily D := fun s ↦ bif s then D.V₁ else D.V₀`, chosen over a `match` so that
51	`boolFamily D false` and `boolFamily D true` reduce by `rfl` and the `⊓` of the two is
52	*syntactically* `D.V₀ ⊓ D.V₁` — which is what lets the landed affineness field `isAffineOpen_inf`
53	be used at the overlap with no transport. That reduction is the whole reason this file is short.
54	
55	## Main declarations
56	
57	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.AffineTwoCover.boolFamily` — the `Bool`-indexed family, with
58	  `boolFamily_false`, `boolFamily_true` and `boolFamily_inf` (all `rfl`).
59	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.AffineTwoCover.selector` — the canonical selector, with
60	  `selector_mem` (the `hmem` clause).
61	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.AffineTwoCover.surjective_selector_iff` — **the side condition,
62	  characterized**: surjectivity is `V₀ ≠ ⊥ ∧ V₀ ≠ ⊤`.
63	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.AffineTwoCover.isAffineOpen_boolFamily` — each chart of the family is
64	  affine, and `isAffineOpen_boolFamily_inf` for the overlap.
65	* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.surjective_selector_comp` — **the producer for the second surjectivity
66	  binder** `hsel'` of `Scheme.map_twoChartClass`, which inbox `I-0688` found had none: selector
67	  surjectivity at the pulled-back end follows from surjectivity at the base end plus surjectivity of
68	  `f.base`.
69	* `AlgebraicGeometry.overSpecMap_eps_eq_overDualNumberZero` — **(3b)**: the `ε ↦ 0` test-object
70	  morphism and the coefficient comparison `overSpecMap k[ε] k` have the *same underlying scheme
71	  morphism*, by `rfl` under the `scoped` `epsAlgebra`. It says **nothing** about the source objects
72	  — see its docstring for the withdrawn claim that it did.
73	* `AlgebraicGeometry.ofHom_algebraMap_self_eq_id` / `specMap_algebraMap_self_eq_id` — the (3c)
74	  measurement: the first is `rfl`, the second is **not** (it needs `Spec.map_id`), which is why
75	  (3c) is a genuine object transport and not free. See that docstring for the retraction it forces.
76	
77	## What this file deliberately does NOT contain
78	
79	An identification of `relCurveMap C k[ε] k` with `(C ◁ overDualNumberZero k).left`. Those two have
80	**different types** — a kernel check refuted the attempt — because their sources are the monoidal
81	unit and `overSpec k k` respectively, which are equal objects but not definitionally equal. Building
82	that transport is (3c), left to a successor with the diagnosis recorded rather than attempted
83	blind; `informal/w5-t4-worksheet.md` §6.23.
84

153	Neither condition is proved here — for the Wave-5 curve both hold (a curve is non-empty; a proper

155	consumer supplies them.
156	
157	**And "both hold for the curve" is at present an argument, not a witness in this project** — the

162	consumer instantiating this lemma at the Wave-5 curve **must still produce those two facts**, and

164	theorem surjective_selector_iff :
165	    Function.Surjective D.selector ↔ D.V₀ ≠ ⊥ ∧ D.V₀ ≠ ⊤ := by
166	  classical
167	  constructor
168	  · intro hs
169	    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
170	    · obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := hs false
171	      rw [selector] at hx
172	      have hxV : x ∈ D.V₀ := by by_contra h; simp [h] at hx

184	        by_contra hc

6	import AlgebraicJacobian.Tangent.DualNumberTestObject
7	import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.JacobianData
8	
9	/-!
10	# The tangent space of the Jacobian at the identity (W5-T5, the scalar-identity spine)
11	
12	The Wave-5 tangent statements phrased against the pinned representability datum
13	`(d : JacobianData C)` (roadmap `AJCR.w5-av.t5`), assembling the generic kit of
14	`Tangent/` into the two forms Wave 5 actually consumes:
15	
16	```
17	Dual κ(e) (m_e/m_e²)  ≃  T_e(d.J)  ≃  ker (Pic⁰(Spec k[ε]) →* Pic⁰(Spec k))
18	```
19	
20	and, under the **one** remaining numerical input, the frozen scalar identity
21	`dim_κ(e) m_e/m_e² = genus C` together with its additive consequence
22	`m_e/m_e² ≃+ H¹(C, 𝒪_C)`.
23	
24	## The scalar-identity-first discipline (w5-worksheet D6), and what it buys
25	
26	The W12 lesson recorded in the worksheet is that dimension transport must go
27	through **one** `finrank` identity, followed by **one** non-canonical `≃+` — not
28	through a chain of additive equivalences each carrying its own linearity
29	bookkeeping. This file is that discipline made structural:
30	
31	* `JacobianData.tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` is the representability leg,
32	  unconditional and sorry-free. It is a bijection of **sets**; it deliberately
33	  does *not* claim to transport dimension (a bare `Equiv` cannot).
34	* `JacobianData.finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_genus` isolates the numerical
35	  content as a **hypothesis** `hdim`. That hypothesis is what the T3/T4 chain must
36	  deliver.
37	* `JacobianData.nonempty_cotangentSpace_addEquiv_h1` then produces the additive
38	  equivalence from the count, once.
39	
40	So the Wave-5 tangent keystone is, at HEAD, reduced to a statement about the
41	`ε`-kernel of `pic0Functor` — **but note precisely which statement**. The
42	`ε`-kernel *bijection* above is not enough on its own: it is a bijection of sets,
43	and `finrank` does not transport along one. What `hdim` needs is the **semilinear
44	comparison** — an additive equivalence plus the intertwining law across
45	`κ(e) ≃+* k` — fed through `finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` (proved
46	below, unconditionally). Stating T3/T4's target as a bare kernel bijection would
47	leave the count unreachable; this is the same residue the AJC sibling isolated as
48	`semilinearComparison_cotangentSpaceDual_h1Cok`. See inbox I-0513.
49	
50	Note that the
51	identity point of `d.J` needs no rationality hypothesis: it is the image of the
52	group-object unit, hence a section, hence automatically `k`-rational
53	(`bijective_algebraMap_residueField_of_section`).
54	
55	## Main declarations
56	
57	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.identitySection` — the `k`-rational identity
58	  point of `d.J`, with `identitySection_isSection`.
59	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.tangentSpaceCotangentDual` — `T_0(d.J)` is the
60	  `κ(e)`-linear dual of the cotangent space at the identity.
61	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` — `T_0(d.J)` is
62	  the `ε`-kernel of `pic0Functor C` (the representability leg, applied).
63	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.cotangentSpaceDual_equiv_pic0Kernel` — the two
64	  composed: the cotangent dual at the identity *is* the `ε`-kernel.
65	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finiteDimensional_cotangentSpace` — the
66	  cotangent space at the identity is finite-dimensional (from
67	  `d.locallyOfFiniteType`).
68	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` —
69	  **unconditional**: `finrank` transports across a scalar *bijection* given an
70	  additive equivalence and the intertwining law. The bridge that makes the count
71	  reachable at all.
72	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_genus` /
73	  `nonempty_cotangentSpace_addEquiv_h1` — the frozen scalar identity and its
74	  additive consequence, each conditional on the T3/T4 semilinear comparison.
75	
76	Reference: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 Thm. 5.11 (arXiv:math/0504020);
77	Milne, "Abelian varieties", Prop. 2.1.
78	-/
79	
80	set_option autoImplicit false
81	set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 3
82	
83	universe u v
84	
85	open CategoryTheory IsLocalRing Opposite
86	
87	namespace AlgebraicGeometry
88	
89	namespace JacobianData
90	
91	variable {k : Type u} [Field k] {C : Over (Spec (.of k))}
92	  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom] [IsProper C.hom] [GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]
93	
94	/-- **The identity point of the Jacobian.** The underlying scheme morphism
95	`Spec k ⟶ d.J.left` of the group-object unit — the `k`-rational point at which
96	Wave 5 computes the tangent space. -/
97	noncomputable def identitySection (d : JacobianData C) : Spec (.of k) ⟶ d.J.left :=
98	  letI := d.grpObj
99	  GroupScheme.identitySection d.J
100	
101	/-- The identity point is a section of the structural morphism (the unit is a
102	morphism of `Over (Spec k)` out of the monoidal unit). -/
103	lemma identitySection_isSection (d : JacobianData C) :
104	    d.identitySection ≫ d.J.hom = 𝟙 (Spec (.of k)) :=
105	  letI := d.grpObj
106	  GroupScheme.identitySection_comp d.J
107	
108	/-- **The tangent space of the Jacobian at the identity, as a cotangent dual**
109	(Kleiman §5 Thm. 5.11, LHS). The pointed dual-number points of `d.J` at the
110	identity form the `κ(e)`-linear dual of the cotangent space `m_e/m_e²`. No
111	rationality hypothesis is needed: the identity point is a section, hence
112	automatically `k`-rational. -/
113	noncomputable def tangentSpaceCotangentDual (d : JacobianData C) :
114	    pointedDualNumberPoints d.J d.identitySection ≃
115	      Module.Dual
116	        (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
117	        (CotangentSpace (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default))) :=
118	  haveI : Subsingleton ↥(Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) :=
119	    inferInstanceAs (Subsingleton (PrimeSpectrum k))
120	  overDualNumberSectionEquivCotangentSpaceDual d.J (d.identitySection_isSection)
121	    (congrArg _ (Subsingleton.elim _ _))
122	
123	/-- **The representability leg, applied** (Kleiman §5 Thm. 5.11): the tangent
124	space of `d.J` at the identity is the **kernel** of the restriction
125	homomorphism
126	
127	```
128	Pic⁰_{C/k}(Spec k[ε]) →* Pic⁰_{C/k}(Spec k)
129	```
130	
131	along the `ε ↦ 0` point. Immediate from `pointedDualNumberPointsEquivKer` at the
132	pinned datum `d.rep`, whose functor is `pic0Functor C` composed with the
133	forgetful functors — note the `forget₂ ⋙ forget` typing of `rep` is exactly what
134	makes the group-valued kernel meaningful, and `JacobianData` owns that massage.
135	
136	⚠ A bijection of **sets**: it does not transport `finrank`. That is the point of
137	the scalar-identity-first discipline — see the module docstring. -/
138	noncomputable def tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel (d : JacobianData C) :
139	    pointedDualNumberPoints d.J d.identitySection ≃
140	      {a : (pic0Functor C).obj (op (overDualNumber k)) //
141	        ((pic0Functor C).map (overDualNumberZero k).op).hom a = 1} :=
142	  pointedDualNumberPointsEquivKer d.J (pic0Functor C) d.rep d.identitySection_isSection
143	
144	/-- **The two legs composed**: the `κ(e)`-linear dual of the cotangent space at
145	the identity of `d.J` *is* the `ε`-kernel of `Pic⁰_{C/k}`. This is the statement
146	the T3/T4 chain computes against, and the one whose dimension T5 counts. -/
147	noncomputable def cotangentSpaceDual_equiv_pic0Kernel (d : JacobianData C) :
148	    Module.Dual
149	        (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
150	        (CotangentSpace (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
151	      ≃ {a : (pic0Functor C).obj (op (overDualNumber k)) //
152	          ((pic0Functor C).map (overDualNumberZero k).op).hom a = 1} :=
153	  d.tangentSpaceCotangentDual.symm.trans d.tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel
154	
155	/-- **Finite-dimensionality of the cotangent space at the identity.** The
156	Jacobian is locally of finite type over `k` by the datum's certificate, hence
157	locally Noetherian, so `m_e/m_e²` is a finite-dimensional `κ(e)`-vector space —
158	the input any dimension count needs. -/
159	theorem finiteDimensional_cotangentSpace (d : JacobianData C) :
160	    FiniteDimensional
161	      (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
162	      (CotangentSpace (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default))) :=
163	  letI := d.locallyOfFiniteType
164	  letI : IsLocallyNoetherian d.J.left := LocallyOfFiniteType.isLocallyNoetherian d.J.hom
165	  inferInstance
166	
167	/-! ## The frozen scalar identity, and the bridge T3/T4 must actually cross
168	
169	Everything above is unconditional. What follows carries the numerical input as an
170	explicit hypothesis, named once:
171	
172	```
173	hdim : Module.finrank κ(e) (m_e/m_e²) = genus C
174	```
175	
176	Keeping it a hypothesis rather than a `sorry` is the w5-worksheet §0(4) rule
177	(never register a staged fact).
178	
179	**What `hdim` needs, stated precisely — the `ε`-kernel bijection alone is NOT
180	enough.** `tangentSpaceEquivPic0Kernel` is a bijection of *sets* (it says so on
181	its own docstring) and a bare `Equiv` does not determine `finrank`. So T3/T4's
182	kernel computation does not by itself give `hdim`: additionally required is an
183	**additive** equivalence together with the intertwining law across the
184	residue-field bijection `κ(e) → k`, because the two sides are modules over
185	genuinely different rings — neither `LinearEquiv.finrank_eq` nor a
186	`restrictScalars` argument applies.
187	
188	`finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul` below is exactly that bridge, and it
189	is unconditional. With it in hand the residual obligation on T3/T4 is the
190	**semilinear comparison**: a scalar bijection `i`, an additive equivalence `j`
191	from `Dual κ(e) (m_e/m_e²)` to `H¹(C,𝒪)`, and `j (r • x) = i r • j x`. That is
192	the honest target to state T3/T4 against — and it is the same residue the AJC
193	sibling isolated (`semilinearComparison_cotangentSpaceDual_h1Cok`), which is why
194	porting the generic kit without this bridge would have left the count
195	unreachable. Found by fresh-context review; see inbox I-0513. -/
196	
197	/-- **`finrank` across a scalar bijection** (the linearity bridge the Wave-5
198	count needs, and the reason the `ε`-kernel *set* bijection is insufficient on its
199	own). If `i : R → R'` is a bijection of scalars, `j : M ≃+ M₁` an additive
200	equivalence, and the two intertwine (`j (r • m) = i r • j m`), then `M` and `M₁`
201	have equal `finrank` over their respective rings.
202	
203	`i` need only be a **bijection**, not a ring homomorphism, and the module
204	structures live over genuinely different rings — which is precisely the situation
205	of the Kleiman §5 Thm. 5.11 count, comparing a `κ(e)`-dimension with a
206	`k`-dimension across `κ(e) ≃+* k`. Mathlib has this at the level of
207	`Module.rank` (`rank_eq_of_equiv_equiv`) but not in `finrank` form; this is the
208	`Module.finrank = toNat ∘ Module.rank` unfolding of it. -/
209	theorem finrank_eq_of_addEquiv_of_bijective_smul
210	    {R : Type*} {R' : Type*} {M M₁ : Type v} [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] [Module R M]
211	    [Semiring R'] [AddCommMonoid M₁] [Module R' M₁]
212	    (i : R → R') (j : M ≃+ M₁) (hi : Function.Bijective i)
213	    (hc : ∀ (r : R) (m : M), j (r • m) = i r • j m) :
214	    Module.finrank R M = Module.finrank R' M₁ := by
215	  unfold Module.finrank
216	  rw [rank_eq_of_equiv_equiv i j hi hc]
217	
218	variable (d : JacobianData C)
219	
220	/-- **The frozen scalar identity** `dim_κ(e) T₀(d.J) = genus C`, conditional on
221	the T3/T4 count. Stated in cotangent form: since `T₀(d.J)` is by
222	`tangentSpaceCotangentDual` the `κ(e)`-linear dual of `m_e/m_e²` and the latter
223	is finite-dimensional (`finiteDimensional_cotangentSpace`), the dual has the same
224	dimension, so this single `finrank` equation *is* the Wave-5 dimension
225	statement — no further transport is needed or wanted (w5-worksheet D6).
226	
227	The hypothesis is exactly what T3/T4 produce; nothing else in Wave 5 needs the
228	`ε`-kernel in any other form. -/
229	theorem finrank_cotangentSpaceDual_eq_genus
230	    (hdim : Module.finrank
231	        (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
232	        (CotangentSpace (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
233	      = genus C) :
234	    Module.finrank
235	        (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))
236	        (Module.Dual
237	          (ResidueField (d.J.left.presheaf.stalk (d.identitySection.base default)))

9	/-!
10	# Tangent-space endgame substrate: the cotangent space vs `H¹` by dimension count
11	
12	The **scalar-identity-first** reduction of the Kleiman §5 Thm.~5.11 tangent
13	keystone (w5-worksheet D6; the W12 lesson: ONE `finrank` identity, then one
14	non-canonical `≃+`). The Wave-5 target asks for an **additive** equivalence
15	between the cotangent space `m_e/m_e²` at the (`k`-rational) identity-section
16	point of the Jacobian and the cohomology `k`-module `H¹(C, 𝒪_C)`,
17	non-canonically (`Nonempty`). Such an equivalence is pure linear algebra once
18	the two sides are
19	
20	1. finite-dimensional vector spaces — over `κ(e)` (local Noetherianity of a
21	   scheme locally of finite type over a field) resp. over `k` (the genus-lane
22	   finiteness of `Sheaf.HModule (C.left.moduleKSheaf k) 1`), with
23	2. `κ(e) ≃+* k` (the image of a section of the structure morphism is a
24	   `k`-rational point, `bijective_algebraMap_residueField_of_section`), and
25	3. equal dimensions.
26	
27	This file provides that reduction as reusable infrastructure:
28	
29	- `Module.nonempty_addEquiv_of_finrank_eq_of_ringEquiv` — finite-dimensional
30	  vector spaces over fields identified by a ring isomorphism are additively
31	  equivalent iff-wise as soon as their dimensions agree (choose bases).
32	- `AlgebraicGeometry.nonempty_cotangentSpaceAddEquiv_of_finrank_eq` — the
33	  scheme-level form: for `X` locally of finite type over `Spec k`, a section
34	  `e` of the structure morphism, and a finite `k`-module `W`, an equality
35	  `dim_{κ(e)} m_e/m_e² = dim_k W` yields `m_e/m_e² ≃+ W`.
36	
37	Consequently the whole content of the Wave-5 tangent keystone (Kleiman FGA
38	Explained 5.11: `T₀ J ≅ H¹(C, 𝒪_C)`) is reduced to the **dimension identity**
39	`dim_{κ(e)} m_e/m_e² = dim_k H¹(C, 𝒪_C)` at `e` the identity section. That
40	identity is what T3/T4 supply: the representability leg (the `ε`-kernel
41	description of the dual-number points, `Tangent/Pic0TangentSpace.lean`) and the
42	truncated-exponential Čech leg (`Tangent/TruncExpCech*.lean`, brick T2, landed).
43	
44	## Provenance (W5-T1 port, cross-project)
45	
46	Ported from `Algebraic-Jacobian-Challenge`,

48	generality; renamed here because the Rebuild reserves `Pic0TangentSpace.lean`
49	for the datum-phrased consumers). See `Tangent/TangentDualNumbers.lean` and
50	inbox `I-0495`. Import list trimmed to what the declarations use.
51	
52	Source: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 Thm.~5.11 (arXiv:math/0504020).
53	-/

62	/-- **Equal-dimension finite-dimensional vector spaces over isomorphic fields
63	are additively equivalent.** For fields `K ≃+* L`, a finite-dimensional
64	`K`-vector space `V` and a finite-dimensional `L`-vector space `W` with
65	`dim_K V = dim_L W` admit an additive equivalence `V ≃+ W`: choose finite
66	bases on both sides (`Module.finBasis`) and transport the coordinates along
67	the field isomorphism componentwise. Non-canonical (basis choice), hence the
68	`Nonempty`. -/
69	theorem Module.nonempty_addEquiv_of_finrank_eq_of_ringEquiv
70	    {K : Type u} {L : Type v} [Field K] [Field L]
71	    {V : Type w} [AddCommGroup V] [Module K V] [FiniteDimensional K V]
72	    {W : Type w'} [AddCommGroup W] [Module L W] [FiniteDimensional L W]
73	    (e : K ≃+* L) (h : Module.finrank K V = Module.finrank L W) :
74	    Nonempty (V ≃+ W) :=
75	  ⟨((Module.finBasis K V).equivFun.toAddEquiv.trans
76	      (AddEquiv.piCongrRight fun _ => e.toAddEquiv)).trans
77	    ((Module.finBasis L W).reindex (finCongr h.symm)).equivFun.toAddEquiv.symm⟩

83	/-- **The cotangent space at a section, additively, by dimension count.** Let
84	`X` be a scheme locally of finite type over `Spec k` and `e` a section of the
85	structure morphism, so that `x = e(*)` is a `k`-rational point and the
86	cotangent space `m_x/m_x²` is a finite-dimensional `κ(x)`-vector space. For
87	any finite `k`-module `W` of the same dimension there is an additive
88	equivalence `m_x/m_x² ≃+ W` (non-canonical: transport bases along
89	`κ(x) ≃+* k`).
90	
91	This is the generic linear-algebra half of Kleiman §5 Thm.~5.11 for
92	`X = d.J`, `W = H¹(C, 𝒪_C)`: it reduces the Wave-5 tangent keystone to the
93	dimension identity `dim_{κ(e)} m_e/m_e² = dim_k H¹(C, 𝒪_C)` (= `genus C`, by
94	the definition of `genus` in `Challenge.lean`). -/
95	theorem nonempty_cotangentSpaceAddEquiv_of_finrank_eq
96	    (X : Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))) [LocallyOfFiniteType X.hom]
97	    {e : Spec (CommRingCat.of k) ⟶ X.left}
98	    (he : e ≫ X.hom = 𝟙 (Spec (CommRingCat.of k)))
99	    (W : Type w) [AddCommGroup W] [Module k W] [Module.Finite k W]
100	    (h : Module.finrank
101	          (ResidueField (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default)))
102	          (CotangentSpace (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default)))
103	        = Module.finrank k W) :
104	    Nonempty
105	      (CotangentSpace (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default)) ≃+ W) := by
106	  haveI : Subsingleton ↥(Spec (CommRingCat.of k)) :=
107	    inferInstanceAs (Subsingleton (PrimeSpectrum k))
108	  -- `e(*)` is a `k`-rational point: `k ≃+* κ(e(*))`.
109	  have hres : Function.Bijective
110	      (algebraMap k (ResidueField (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default)))) :=
111	    bijective_algebraMap_residueField_of_section X he
112	      (congrArg _ (Subsingleton.elim _ _))
113	  -- the cotangent space is finite-dimensional over the residue field
114	  letI : IsLocallyNoetherian X.left := LocallyOfFiniteType.isLocallyNoetherian X.hom
115	  haveI : FiniteDimensional
116	      (ResidueField (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default)))
117	      (CotangentSpace (X.left.presheaf.stalk (e.base default))) :=
118	    inferInstance
119	  exact Module.nonempty_addEquiv_of_finrank_eq_of_ringEquiv
120	    (residueFieldEquivOfBijective hres).symm h

122	/-! ## Pointed dual-number points along an open immersion
123	
124	A clopen-transport connector for the Kleiman §5 Thm.~5.11 dimension identity:
125	the Zariski tangent space of an open subgroup scheme at a point is the tangent
126	space of the ambient scheme there, because `Spec k[ε]` is a one-point scheme,
127	so a pointed dual-number point of the ambient scheme at a point of an open
128	subscheme factors (uniquely) through the open immersion. Stated for an
129	arbitrary morphism of `Over (Spec k)`-schemes whose underlying morphism is an
130	open immersion.
131	
132	The Rebuild's `pic0Functor` is degree-zero *by definition* (a subgroup of
133	`picEt`, not an identity component carved out of a larger Picard scheme), so
134	this connector is **not** on the Rebuild's critical path the way it is on the
135	sibling's — it is kept because it is generic, cheap, and the natural tool if a
136	later lane does introduce an open immersion `d.J ↪ (something bigger)`. -/
137	
138	/-- The spectrum of the dual numbers over a field is a one-point space: every
139	prime of `k[ε]` is the maximal ideal, since every nonunit `x` has vanishing
140	constant component, hence `x² = 0` lies in every prime. -/
141	instance DualNumber.instSubsingletonPrimeSpectrum :
142	    Subsingleton (PrimeSpectrum (DualNumber k)) := by
143	  constructor
144	  have key : ∀ p : PrimeSpectrum (DualNumber k),
145	      p.asIdeal = maximalIdeal (DualNumber k) := by
146	    intro p
147	    refine le_antisymm (le_maximalIdeal p.isPrime.ne_top) fun x hx => ?_
148	    have hfst : TrivSqZeroExt.fst x = 0 := by
149	      by_contra h0
150	      exact hx (TrivSqZeroExt.isUnit_iff_isUnit_fst.mpr (isUnit_iff_ne_zero.mpr h0))
151	    have hsq : x * x = 0 := by
152	      have hxr : x = TrivSqZeroExt.inr (TrivSqZeroExt.snd x) := by
153	        conv_lhs => rw [← TrivSqZeroExt.inl_fst_add_inr_snd_eq x]
154	        rw [hfst, TrivSqZeroExt.inl_zero, zero_add]
155	      rw [hxr, TrivSqZeroExt.inr_mul_inr]
156	    exact p.isPrime.mem_of_pow_mem 2 (by rw [pow_two, hsq]; exact p.asIdeal.zero_mem)
157	  intro p q
158	  exact PrimeSpectrum.ext ((key p).trans (key q).symm)
159	
160	/-- **Pointed dual-number points transport along open immersions.** For a
161	morphism `f : X ⟶ Y` of schemes over `Spec k` whose underlying scheme
162	morphism is an open immersion, and a `k`-point `e` of `X`, composition with
163	`f` identifies the pointed dual-number points of `X` at `e(*)` with those of
164	`Y` at `f(e(*))`: since `Spec k[ε]` is a one-point scheme, any dual-number
165	point of `Y` landing at `f(e(*))` has range inside the open image of `f`,
166	hence lifts uniquely (`IsOpenImmersion.lift`). -/
167	noncomputable def pointedDualNumberPointsEquivOfOpenImmersion
168	    {X Y : Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))} (f : X ⟶ Y) [IsOpenImmersion f.left]
169	    (e : Spec (CommRingCat.of k) ⟶ X.left) :
170	    {g : Spec (CommRingCat.of (DualNumber k)) ⟶ X.left //
171	        g ≫ X.hom = Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k (DualNumber k)))
172	          ∧ g.base (closedPoint (DualNumber k)) = e.base default}
173	      ≃ {g : Spec (CommRingCat.of (DualNumber k)) ⟶ Y.left //
174	        g ≫ Y.hom = Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k (DualNumber k)))
175	          ∧ g.base (closedPoint (DualNumber k)) = (e ≫ f.left).base default} where
176	  toFun g :=
177	    ⟨g.1 ≫ f.left,
178	      by rw [Category.assoc, Over.w f]; exact g.2.1,
179	      by rw [Scheme.Hom.comp_apply, g.2.2, Scheme.Hom.comp_apply]⟩
180	  invFun h :=
181	    have hrange : Set.range h.1.base ⊆ Set.range f.left.base := by
182	      rintro - ⟨t, rfl⟩
183	      refine ⟨e.base default, ?_⟩
184	      have ht : t = closedPoint (DualNumber k) :=
185	        Subsingleton.elim (α := PrimeSpectrum (DualNumber k)) t _
186	      rw [ht, h.2.2, Scheme.Hom.comp_apply]
187	    ⟨IsOpenImmersion.lift f.left h.1 hrange,
188	      by rw [← Over.w f, ← Category.assoc, IsOpenImmersion.lift_fac]; exact h.2.1,
189	      by
190	        apply (Scheme.Hom.isOpenEmbedding f.left).injective
191	        rw [← Scheme.Hom.comp_apply, IsOpenImmersion.lift_fac, h.2.2,
192	          Scheme.Hom.comp_apply]⟩
193	  left_inv g :=
194	    Subtype.ext (by rw [← cancel_mono f.left]; exact IsOpenImmersion.lift_fac _ _ _)
195	  right_inv h := Subtype.ext (IsOpenImmersion.lift_fac _ _ _)

9	# Smoothness of the Jacobian (W5-S2), and the shape of the relative-dimension assembly
10	
11	Brick S2 of the Wave-5 abelian-variety package (roadmap `AJCR.w5-av.s2`):
12	`Smooth d.J.hom` for the pinned representability datum `(d : JacobianData C)`,
13	via mathlib's group-scheme smoothness criterion.
14	
15	## Why this is one line, and what it costs
16	
17	`smooth_of_grpObj` (`Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/Group/Smooth.lean:64`) needs three
18	hypotheses on `f`, and the datum supplies two of them outright:
19	
20	* `[LocallyOfFiniteType f]` — `d.locallyOfFiniteType`, a construction certificate;
21	* `[GrpObj (Over.mk f)]` — `d.grpObj`. Note the **keying**: instance search does
22	  not unfold `Over.mk` on its own, so the group structure must be ascribed at the
23	  `Over.mk d.J.hom` spelling. This is pure defeq (`Over.mk d.J.hom` *is* `d.J` by
24	  structure eta) and `Picard/JacobianData.lean` machine-checks exactly this as its
25	  η-defeq smoke test 2;
26	* `[GeometricallyReduced f]` — brick **S1**, which is *not* proved here. It stays
27	  an instance argument, so this file is unconditional in the datum and every
28	  consumer sees the S1 dependency in its own signature.
29	
30	Geometric (rather than bare) reducedness is intrinsic to mathlib's route, not an
31	artefact: the proof base-changes to `AlgebraicClosure k`, runs the homogeneity
32	argument there — translating the smooth locus by `GrpObj.mulRight` until it meets
33	any prescribed closed point — and descends along
34	`@Surjective ⊓ @Flat ⊓ @QuasiCompact`. That is also why S1 is naturally stated
35	geometrically; see `informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §1–§2.
36

38	
39	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.smooth` — `Smooth d.J.hom`, given S1.
40	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.smooth_of_smoothOfRelativeDimension` — the
41	  degradation direction of the frozen numeral, recorded so that S3's consumers
42	  need not re-derive `Smooth` from `SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C)`.
43	
44	The S3 assembly itself (`SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C) d.J.hom`) is
45	**worksheet-first** and its route is frozen in `informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §3;
46	the short version is that mathlib's `SmoothOfRelativeDimension` is a *pointwise,
47	local-at-source* condition, so no "relative dimension is locally constant"
48	theorem is needed — translation homogeneity (X2) transports the identity count
49	(T5) to the other points. No Lean is written for S3 here: its numeral waits on
50	T3/T4.
51	
52	Reference: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 `cor:sm` (arXiv:math/0504020);
53	Milne, "Abelian varieties", Prop. 2.1.
54	-/

12	
13	The top-level Wave-5 statement, assembled from the legs proved across `Tangent/`
14	and `AbelianVariety/`, and **conditional on exactly the inputs that are still
15	open**. Following `informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §2.1 recommendation (a): assemble
16	the package now with the open inputs as explicit arguments, rather than wait —
17	that unblocks everything downstream of the assembly and keeps the residual
18	obligations visible in the signatures instead of buried in `sorry`s.
19	
20	## What is closed and what is open
21	
22	Closed, unconditionally, at the datum:
23	
24	* `IsSeparated d.J.hom` — X1, group-theoretic (`AbelianVariety/GroupSeparated.lean`).
25	* `LocallyOfFiniteType` / `QuasiCompact` — the datum's construction certificates.
26	* the tangent identifications `T₀(d.J) ≃ Dual κ(e) (m_e/m_e²) ≃ ker(Pic⁰(k[ε]) → Pic⁰(k))`
27	  — T1/T5 (`Tangent/Pic0TangentSpace.lean`).
28	
29	Open, and therefore *arguments* here rather than hypotheses discharged elsewhere:
30	
31	1. `AbelSourceData d` — the proper `Div^d`-source with its Abel morphism (**P1**,
32	   a cross-wave gate on the divisor-representability shapes). Supplies properness
33	   (P3) and geometric irreducibility (G1).
34	2. `GeometricallyReduced d.J.hom` — **S1**. See `informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §2:
35	   its remaining content is the reduced-stalk-at-the-identity statement, gated on
36	   the T3/T4 `ε`-kernel computation, plus a transcendental-extension step that the
37	   pinned mathlib does not have.
38	3. `hdim` — the T3/T4 numeral `dim_κ(e) m_e/m_e² = genus C`.
39	
40	## Why `SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C)` is *not* claimed here
41	
42	S3's route is frozen in `informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §3 and is genuinely
43	available — mathlib's `SmoothOfRelativeDimension` is pointwise and
44	local-at-source, so translation homogeneity (X2) transporting the identity count
45	(T5) is the whole uniformity argument, with no locally-constant-dimension theorem
46	needed. But it consumes `hdim` *chartwise*, through
47	`IsStandardSmoothOfRelativeDimension.iff_of_isStandardSmooth`, and that chart
48	bookkeeping is real work that the numeral does not yet support. Claiming it now
49	would mean either a `sorry` or a hypothesis so strong it assumes the conclusion;
50	neither is honest. `isAbelianVariety_of_abelSource` below therefore delivers the
51	*proper + smooth + geometrically irreducible group scheme* package — everything
52	except the frozen numeral — and `smoothOfRelativeDimension_statement` records
53	what remains, as a `Prop`-valued abbreviation so that the residual obligation has
54	a name and a home.
55	
56	## Main declarations
57	
58	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.isProper_and_smooth_of_abelSource` — proper and
59	  smooth over `k`, given (1) and (2).
60	* `AlgebraicGeometry.JacobianData.isAbelianVariety_of_abelSource` — the full
61	  package: separated, proper, smooth, geometrically irreducible.
62	
63	Reference: Kleiman, "The Picard scheme", §5 `cor:sm` (arXiv:math/0504020);
64	Milne, "Abelian varieties", Thm. 1.6 and Prop. 2.1.
65	-/

83	reducedness (S1). Properness is P3 (`isProper_of_abelSource`: X1 + P2 + the
84	local-finite-type certificate) and smoothness is S2 (`JacobianData.smooth`, i.e.

88	    IsProper d.J.hom ∧ Smooth d.J.hom :=
89	  ⟨isProper_of_abelSource a, d.smooth⟩

92	(P1) and geometric reducedness (S1): the representing object of the datum is a
93	separated, proper, smooth, geometrically irreducible group scheme over `k`.
94	
95	The group structure itself is `d.grpObj` and is not restated in the conjunction;
96	what the four conjuncts add is exactly the "abelian variety" content beyond being
97	a group object. The remaining Wave-5 item after this is the *frozen numeral*
98	(relative dimension `genus C`), recorded in `smoothOfRelativeDimension_statement`
99	below. -/
100	theorem isAbelianVariety_of_abelSource (a : AbelSourceData d)
101	    [GeometricallyReduced d.J.hom] :
102	    IsSeparated d.J.hom ∧ IsProper d.J.hom ∧ Smooth d.J.hom
103	      ∧ GeometricallyIrreducible d.J.hom :=
104	  ⟨d.isSeparated, isProper_of_abelSource a, d.smooth,
105	    geometricallyIrreducible_of_abelSource a⟩
106	
107	/-- **The residual Wave-5 obligation, named** (S3, roadmap `AJCR.w5-av.s3`): that
108	`d.J` is smooth of relative dimension `genus C` over `k`. Its route is frozen in
109	`informal/w5-s-worksheet.md` §3 (pointwise charts + X2 translation transport of
110	the T5 identity count; **no** rel-dim descent and **no**
111	locally-constant-dimension theorem needed), and it consumes the T3/T4 numeral
112	chartwise.
113	
114	Kept as a named `Prop` rather than a `sorry`ed theorem so that the obligation is
115	citable, greppable, and machine-checkable when discharged, without registering a
116	staged fact (w5-worksheet §0(4)). -/

118	  SmoothOfRelativeDimension (genus C) d.J.hom

121	`genus C` implies smoothness, so the Abel source is the only remaining input for
122	properness and geometric irreducibility, and `GeometricallyReduced` is no longer
123	needed as a separate hypothesis — it follows from smoothness

125

127	dependency direction explicit and prevents the circularity S1 invites (S2 derives
128	`Smooth` *from* `GeometricallyReduced`, so the converse must only ever be used
129	on the S3 side). -/
